model. A real pipeline is a chain of dozens or hundreds of nodes that runs every night without you. When something breaks at 3 a.m., the questions are different: Which node failed first? What did dbt do with everything below it? Which dashboards show yesterday's numbers now? Can I re-run only what failed? Can I get production tables into my schema to investigate, without rebuilding everything?

In this chapter you break the practice pipeline in the middle on purpose (a bad column, a failing test, a new status value in the raw data, a broken hook, a locked database) and watch exactly how dbt reacts. Then you build
for the first time with all its tests, keep its artifacts, and use
to copy production objects into development. Along the way you will hit two real problems that the reference project hit, and fix one of them.
For the exam, topic 4 ("Troubleshooting and optimizing dbt pipelines") has two objectives: failure points in the DAG and
. The questions are concrete: "model X fails, which nodes run?", "what does
create on Snowflake? on Postgres?", "clone or defer?".
When a node fails, dbt marks it
for a test), skips everything downstream of it, and keeps running every independent branch, unless you ask it to stop everything with
, and the production run's artifacts are what later commands (clone, defer, retry, state) compare against.

reads a state manifest and creates the selected models, seeds and snapshots in your target schema, as zero-copy clones of the production tables where the platform supports it (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery) or as views that point to the production objects elsewhere (DuckDB, Postgres).

Think of a car factory line. Parts arrive from suppliers (sources), stations assemble them step by step (models), and inspectors check the result at several points (tests). The line can stop because a supplier sends late or wrong parts, because one station is badly set up, because an inspector rejects a piece, because the electricity fails, or because the morning set-up routine (hooks) went wrong. A good factory knows which station stopped, and does not keep assembling cars on top of a broken piece.

A library has a rare, heavy book. You want it on your desk. Option 1, a
: the library gives you a new catalogue card that points to the same pages; nothing is photocopied, and if you write in your copy, only the pages you change are copied for you. Option 2, a
: you get a note that says "the book is on shelf 12 of the main room"; every time you read it, you walk to the original. Option 3, rebuilding the model: you write the book again from the sources.
uses the first option when the warehouse can, otherwise the second one. It never does the third one.
